# ALS evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025; this does not remove knowledge already in a model's training. Co-Scientist outputs are not included.

## Research question

Propose one specific, testable hypothesis connecting phosphorylation of a nuclear-pore-complex nucleoporin to ALS-related neuronal dysfunction. Explain the causal chain, distinguish an initiating mechanism from a downstream response, and propose an experimental strategy that discriminates the hypothesis from an alternative. Identify supported premises, speculative bridges, and a falsifying observation. This adapts Co-Scientist Supplementary Note 10; nucleoporin phosphorylation is not supplied as an established ALS cause.

## S1 — TDP-43 and nuclear-pore dysfunction

Chou et al. (2018), *TDP-43 pathology disrupts nuclear pore complexes and nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS/FTD*. Nature Neuroscience. DOI: `10.1038/s41593-017-0047-3`; PMID: `29311743`; PMCID: `PMC5800968`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29311743/).

Nuclear-pore and transport components were associated with insoluble TDP-43 aggregates. Disease-linked TDP-43 disrupted nucleoporin localization and nuclear transport in experimental cell systems; relevant pore pathology was observed in ALS tissue. This supports examining the connection between TDP-43 pathology and transport disruption. It does not identify a nucleoporin phosphorylation event as the initiating cause or establish the same sequence in every ALS subtype.

## S2 — C9orf72-associated transport defects

Zhang et al. (2015), *The C9orf72 repeat expansion disrupts nucleocytoplasmic transport*. Nature. DOI: `10.1038/nature14973`; PMID: `26308891`; PMCID: `PMC4800742`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26308891/).

Expanded C9orf72 repeat RNA was linked to altered RanGAP localization and impaired nuclear import in models and patient-derived neurons. Manipulations of transport or repeat-RNA-associated mechanisms modified model phenotypes. This supplies a genetic-context-specific route to transport dysfunction. It does not show that sporadic ALS arises by the same route or directly establish a nucleoporin phosphorylation mechanism.

## S3 — A stress-granule-independent route

Gasset-Rosa et al. (2019), *Cytoplasmic TDP-43 De-mixing Independent of Stress Granules Drives Inhibition of Nuclear Import, Loss of Nuclear TDP-43, and Cell Death*. Neuron. DOI: `10.1016/j.neuron.2019.02.038`; PMID: `30853299`; PMCID: `PMC6548321`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30853299/).

Persistent cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies could form independently of conventional stress granules. They recruited or mislocalized transport-associated proteins and were associated with impaired transport, nuclear TDP-43 depletion, and cell death. Phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulated in these assemblies. That is not itself evidence of nucleoporin phosphorylation. The experimental perturbations do not establish that every physiological ALS trajectory begins in this way.

## S4 — A stress-granule-associated route

Zhang et al. (2018), *Stress Granule Assembly Disrupts Nucleocytoplasmic Transport*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.025`; PMID: `29628143`; PMCID: `PMC6083872`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29628143/).

Cellular stress recruited transport factors into stress granules and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport. Altering stress-granule assembly modified transport defects and disease-model phenotypes. This provides a sequestration-based alternative to an intrinsic pore-modification hypothesis. Read alongside S3, it does not justify assuming that conventional stress granules are required for every TDP-43-associated transport defect.

## Evidence boundaries

- These selected passages do not establish that nucleoporin phosphorylation initiates ALS. Label a proposed kinase, modification site, or interaction as an assumption unless a supplied source supports it.
- Specify the ALS context; do not assume a universal mechanism across genetic and sporadic disease.
- Distinguish pore alteration, transport-factor sequestration, and failure secondary to broader stress.
- Explain temporal and perturbational evidence that would distinguish cause from consequence.
- Propose a research hypothesis rather than claiming a mechanism or treatment has been validated.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Hypothesis title: Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates nuclear transport failure upstream of TDP-43 condensate sequestration in TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons. Mechanism and causal chain: In stressed motor neurons carrying TDP-43 pathology, an aberrant kinase event phosphorylates the FG-repeat nucleoporin NUP98 at sites that normally mediate regulated pore disassembly. In interphase neurons, this phosphorylation weakens NUP98 association with the pore scaffold, destabilizes the FG permeability barrier, and reduces Ran-dependent nuclear import and export. Impaired export then secondarily depletes nuclear TDP-43 and accelerates cytoplasmic TDP-43 accumulation. On this model, nucleoporin phosphorylation is the initiating lesion; sequestration of transport factors into stress granules or cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies is a parallel amplifier or downstream consequence, not the first cause. Supported premises (from the packet only): TDP-43 pathology is associated with nucleoporin mislocalization and impaired nucleocytoplasmic transport in ALS models and tissue, justifying a pore-centric mechanism [S1]. Transport disruption is sufficient to produce ALS-relevant phenotypes in a defined genetic context, including RanGAP mislocalization, and manipulating transport modifies phenotypes [S2]. Cytoplasmic TDP-43 assemblies that form independently of conventional stress granules impair import and deplete nuclear TDP-43, and phosphorylated TDP-43 accumulates in those assemblies; however, that phosphorylation is on TDP-43, not on a nucleoporin [S3]. Stress-granule assembly itself can disrupt transport, providing a competing sequestration route [S4]. No packet source establishes any nucleoporin phosphorylation event in ALS; the hypothesis intentionally extends beyond the supplied evidence. Speculative bridges, explicitly labeled as assumptions: (1) NUP98 is known to undergo mitotic phosphorylation that promotes its dissociation from pores; this is unverified prior knowledge recalled from outside the packet and is not linked to disease by S1-S4. (2) The identity of the neuronal kinase (candidate examples: a p38/MAPK-family or CDK-family enzyme) is an assumption. (3) The claims that site-specific NUP98 phosphorylation alone is sufficient to impair Ran-dependent transport, and that it temporally precedes nuclear TDP-43 depletion, are assumptions with no packet support. Alternative explanations to be discriminated: (a) Sequestration-first: cytoplasmic TDP-43 condensates [S3] or stress granules [S4] physically retain importins and Ran-pathway components, so any pore alteration is secondary. (b) Occlusion-first: insoluble TDP-43 aggregates directly bind and mislocalize pore components [S1]. (c) Epiphenomenon: kinase activation during stress merely marks damage, and phosphorylation neither causes nor sustains transport failure. Discriminating preclinical strategy: Use human iPSC-derived motor neurons in a TDP-43-relevant context (e.g., inducible TDP-43 nuclear depletion and, separately, C9orf72-expansion lines) with isogenic controls. (1) Temporal mapping: perform time-resolved phosphoproteomics on enriched nuclear-envelope fractions after acute stress or TDP-43 perturbation and develop phospho-specific antibodies against candidate NUP98 sites; detect whether NUP98 phosphorylation precedes RanGAP mislocalization, import failure, and nuclear TDP-43 loss. (2) Perturbational sufficiency and necessity: engineer knock-in phospho-null (S-to-A) and phospho-mimetic (S-to-E/D) NUP98 alleles. The hypothesis predicts phospho-null NUP98 preserves import reporters and nuclear TDP-43 and delays cell death even while stress granules or TDP-43 assemblies still form, whereas phospho-mimetic NUP98 in otherwise healthy neurons should impair transport before any detectable cytoplasmic TDP-43 aggregation or stress-granule marker recruitment; this sufficiency outcome is not predicted by sequestration-based models. (3) Dual live readouts in the same cells: simultaneously image NLS-cargo import and stress-granule/condensate markers; acute kinase inhibition should rescue transport without requiring condensate dissolution if phosphorylation is initiating, whereas rescue only upon condensate dissolution would support the sequestration alternative. (4) Window-of-inhibition experiments: early kinase inhibition should be protective if phosphorylation is upstream. Falsifying observation: The hypothesis is falsified if phospho-null NUP98 knock-in neurons fail to preserve transport under TDP-43 stress, phospho-mimetic NUP98 does not impair transport in healthy neurons, and NUP98 phosphorylation is detected only after import defects and nuclear TDP-43 loss are already established. Together these results would indicate pore phosphorylation is a consequence of sequestration or stress rather than the initiating event. Limitations: The packet is not a comprehensive review, and the kinase, site, temporal precedence, and sufficiency claims are assumptions. The hypothesis is restricted to TDP-43-positive ALS and does not claim universality; C9orf72 disease involves additional transport-affecting routes [S2], and other subtypes were not characterized here. iPSC motor-neuron immaturity, redundancy among FG-nucleoporins, and cell-to-cell heterogeneity constrain interpretation, so negative results must be checked across multiple nucleoporins and patient lines before any conclusion is drawn.

Ranked proposal:
Stress-activated phosphorylation of the FG-nucleoporin NUP98 initiates nuclear transport failure upstream of TDP-43 condensate sequestration in TDP-43-positive ALS motor neurons
